findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses numeric keys but the endpoint orders by a datetime column
findings.body:
`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `getattr(item, self.key)`. The audit log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`, so the value is a `datetime`. When the first page has any rows, `build_cursor` calls the key function and raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`, which returns a 500.

`value_from_cursor` has the same problem: it returns the raw integer cursor value. `build_queryset` then emits `WHERE datetime <= <int>`, which Postgres rejects.

The class copies `Paginator`'s integer-key logic instead of `DateTimePaginator`'s (multiplier plus `fromtimestamp`). The optimized audit-log path cannot work for any non-empty organization.

findings.title: User-controlled negative cursor offsets are passed straight into queryset slicing
findings.body:
When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]`. The offset comes directly from the client-supplied `cursor` query parameter.

The comment says "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically". That is false: Django raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")`, so any such request is an unhandled 500.

The stated intent, "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds", is itself a red flag. Pagination bounds should never be bypassable by crafting a cursor. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError`, as `OffsetPaginator` and `ChainPaginator` already do.

This audit-log/pagination change is also unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (spans buffer eviction) and should not ride along in it.

findings.title: Dereferences organization_context.member unconditionally; crashes when member is None
findings.body:
`enable_advanced` is computed on every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not requested. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for callers that are not org members, such as API-key or org-auth-token requests where `request.user` is anonymous.

For those callers `request.user.is_superuser` is False, so `organization_context.member.has_global_access` raises `AttributeError` and the endpoint returns a 500. This regresses audit-log access for existing token-based integrations.

Compute this only inside the `use_optimized` branch and guard against `member is None`.

findings.title: Privilege gate uses raw is_superuser flag and has_global_access, not an admin check
findings.body:
The comment says the advanced paginator is for "authorized administrators", but neither check actually restricts it to admins.

- `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw DB flag. Sentry requires `is_active_superuser(request)`, an active superuser session, before granting superuser powers, and this bypasses that.
- `has_global_access` is true for every ordinary member in organizations with open membership (`allow_joinleave`), so it is not an admin check either.

The gate therefore exposes the "advanced" negative-offset behavior to far more users than intended.

findings.title: Redis key type changes from SET to ZSET with no migration; WRONGTYPE errors during rollout
findings.body:
Segment keys `span-buf:s:*` were Redis SETs (`sadd`/`scard`/`sunionstore`/`sscan`). They are now ZSETs (`zadd`/`zcard`/`zunionstore`/`zscan`) under the same key names.

Existing keys survive up to `redis_ttl` (3600s) and stay referenced from the flush queues. During and after deploy:
- New consumers will hit `WRONGTYPE` on `zadd` (pipeline raises), on `zcard`/`zunionstore` inside the Lua script, and on `zscan` in `_load_segment_data`.
- Old consumers still running during the rolling deploy will hit the same errors on keys written by new ones.

This crashes the span consumer and can drop or duplicate segments. The change needs a new key prefix or version, or a drain/flush plan, before rollout.

findings.title: Span eviction silently drops data with no metric or log, and can evict the root span
findings.body:
`zpopmin` removes the spans with the smallest `end_timestamp_precise` whenever a segment exceeds 1000 spans. The previous code emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error. Now spans are discarded with no signal, so data loss in production is invisible.

Eviction is purely by end time, so a segment/root span that ends before 1000 of its children can be evicted. The segment is then flushed with no span marked `is_segment`, even though the `hrs` flag says it has a root.

The `span-buf:sr` redirect entries of evicted spans are never `hdel`'d in `done_flush_segments`, because only flushed spans are cleaned. They linger until the hash TTL lapses.

At minimum, return the eviction count from the script and emit a metric.

findings.title: max_segment_spans config is now dead; Lua hardcodes a different limit
findings.body:
`SpansBuffer.__init__` still accepts and stores `max_segment_spans` (default 1001), but nothing reads it after the Python-side check was removed.

The effective cap is the literal `1000` hardcoded in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` will see no effect, and the defaults already disagree (1001 vs 1000).

Pass the limit to the script as an ARGV, or remove the parameter.

findings.title: ZUNIONSTORE default SUM aggregation corrupts scores for duplicate members
findings.body:
`zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` uses the default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the same payload is present in both sets, for example after a Kafka redelivery, its score becomes the sum of the two end timestamps (about 2x).

That breaks the end-timestamp ordering the new `zpopmin` eviction relies on: such members effectively become un-evictable while legitimately later spans get evicted. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`) so the score remains a timestamp. The same applies to the `parent_key` union on line 53.

findings.title: No tests for the new eviction behavior or the optimized audit-log paginator
findings.body:
The PR's headline feature, evicting spans beyond 1000 during insert, has no test.

Nothing covers:
- a segment exceeding the cap, or which spans survive;
- that redirect and queue keys are cleaned afterwards;
- interaction with the root span.

The tests only add `end_timestamp_precise` to existing fixtures.

Likewise there are no tests for `OptimizedCursorPaginator` or the `optimized_pagination=true` path of the audit log endpoint. A single test there would have caught the `math.floor(datetime)` TypeError and the negative-slice ValueError.

findings.title: BasePaginator negative-offset change is inconsistent and its comment is misleading
findings.body:
This change affects every endpoint using `Paginator`/`DateTimePaginator`. The comment claims it "allow[s] negative offsets", but it does the opposite for forward cursors: they are silently clamped to 0.

For prev cursors the negative offset is still passed to the queryset and Django raises `ValueError` (a 500). The clamped forward case also feeds the original negative `cursor.offset` into `build_cursor`, so the next cursor's offset is wrong and rows get skipped or repeated.

The matching comment added in `utils/cursors.py` describes behavior that doesn't exist. Negative offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` instead.
